Re-entrant publish raises rather than cascading. Handlers RETURN follow-ups, which are checked against a default-deny category matrix where every allowance carries a written reason, and bounded at depth 2. health -> notifications only; notifications terminal.

An event payload containing a credential shape, or a field named like one, is REFUSED rather than redacted -- at any nesting depth. Phase 6's shapes are reused so there is one answer in the codebase to what a credential looks like.

8.name: Build the Job System

requirements.evidence: All eleven manifest fields on a frozen Job; all twelve states with a transition TABLE rather than scattered conditionals. Terminal states have no outgoing edge; FAILED deliberately does, because a retry is a real thing.

Expiry is re-checked at dispatch, delivery, start and authorization -- not once at dispatch. The named test is the reconnection story: a device dispatched at 21:00 that comes back at 21:30 holding the job raises JobExpired instead of running, and the job is EXPIRED afterwards.
The same (user, idempotency_key) returns the same job rather than creating a second one, including after that job has SUCCEEDED. Scoped per user, so two users' keys cannot collide.

Every dispatch mints a delivery token; start, succeed and fail all refuse a stale one. A redispatch invalidates the previous token, which is what makes a lost acknowledgement recoverable rather than a double completion.

deliver() is a no-op on repeat -- duplicate delivery is the normal case on a flaky link. A lease that runs out sends the job back to the queue with attempts raised and the token cleared; a job that had already started is recorded FAILED('acknowledgement_lost') first rather than silently requeued.

Retries stop at max_attempts (3) and end EXPIRED with a reason naming which limit ran out. Cancellation works from every non-terminal state including DISPATCHED, and start() re-checks state rather than trusting what the device was told.

Phase 8 is Phase 7's first producer. remote_jobs.job_created and remote_jobs.job_state_changed carry job_id and status; a test asserts arguments never appear in a payload. The bus would refuse a credential anyway.
Python 607/607 (was 568), plugin 146/146 unchanged, policy check 390/390, audit check OK, capability check agrees, secret scan clean.

limitations: NOTHING RUNS. There is no dispatcher process, no transport, and no device on the other end. Phase 5's engine still denies any request whose target is not its origin, so no job can legitimately be remote yet. This is the queue and its rules.

Retry after a lost acknowledgement can double-execute unless the TARGET DEVICE honours the idempotency key. The queue cannot tell 'the device never got it' from 'the device did it and the answer was lost'; it records the difference (FAILED with acknowledgement_lost vs delivery_unacknowledged) and retries anyway. Device-side deduplication is a Phase 44 requirement and nothing enforces it today.
A job that legitimately started before its TTL may report success afterwards. Refusing a late success would leave a half-done delete with no record that it happened; the alternative was judged worse.
A job out of retries ends in EXPIRED, because the manifest's twelve states have no 'exhausted' and FAILED is the state a retry comes back from. The reason field distinguishes them.
The queue is in-memory and not thread-safe. Durability and concurrency belong to the backend (Phases 10-11) and to whatever owns a runloop.
followUps: Phase 44 (Mac Remote Connection Foundation) must implement device-side idempotency-key deduplication before any retry path goes live, and must re-check job expiry on the device as well -- the queue can only refuse what it is asked about.
sweep(now) needs an owner. Core has no runloop by design; whichever adapter gains one has to call it, or lost leases are never noticed.

12.name: Secret and Credential Vault

requirements.evidence: A data key per credential encrypts the secret; a KEK held by the KMS encrypts the data key. The row stores ciphertext and the WRAPPED key. KmsPort has no method that returns a KEK, so 'master keys outside PostgreSQL' is a property of the interface rather than a deployment note -- asserted by a test.

credential_id, user_id, provider, scopes, encrypted_refresh_token, key_version, created_at, updated_at, revoked_at. No field holds a plaintext token and no code path writes one; the Phase 11 table matches.

RefusingCipher is the default and raises. An unauthenticated cipher is refused at construction -- confidentiality without integrity means an attacker who can write to the database can flip bits in a token. Tests inject TestOnlyCipher, named so it is obvious in a stack trace if it ever reaches somewhere real.

user, connection and provider are the associated data, so copying encrypted_refresh_token into another user's row yields a token that fails authentication rather than decrypting under their name. Tampering with a byte is detected.

rotate_key re-wraps every data key under the current KEK; the ciphertext is byte-identical afterwards and the secret still decrypts. Idempotent. A retired KEK cannot unwrap -- losing access is the correct failure there, guessing is not.

Decryption returns a context manager: inside the `with` the bytes exist, at the end the buffer is overwritten and further reads raise. The wrapper refuses repr, str, format, bytes(), comparison and hashing -- the three ways a secret reaches a log are an f-string, a debugger, and json.dumps of a dict somebody thought was safe.

No module operation and no route names a secret-returning operation, asserted over Phase 10's tables. metadata() is a view rather than a filtered dump, so adding a field to the record does not silently add it to a response. And a borrowed secret is not JSON, so Phase 3's bundle, Phase 6's details and Phase 7's payload each refuse it by type -- tested on both the name path and the type path.

delete_connection revokes every credential under it in the same call, not through a job or an event -- anything asynchronous leaves a window in which a deleted connection can still refresh. A deleted connection cannot be given a new credential either. This closes Phase 9's last pending invariant: EXPECTED_PENDING is now 0.

The default raises rather than encrypting, so a deployment that forgets cannot store a credential at all -- but nothing here has ever encrypted anything with a production-grade cipher.

InProcessKms is a stand-in, not a KMS. Its wrap is HMAC-derived-keystream XOR, which is sufficient for wrapping 32 random bytes and is not a general-purpose cipher. Production uses the platform KMS through the same port.

13.name: Authentication

requirements.evidence: sign_in authenticates an ACCOUNT; device_id is recorded on the session and is never consulted in deciding whether the sign-in succeeds. Tested in both directions -- a session can exist without a device, and a device cannot be the proof.

CONNECTOR_PROVIDERS sits next to the mechanism registry; mechanism('google') raises ConnectorIsNotALogin, and constructing a Mechanism named after a connector raises at declaration. Being able to read someone's Gmail is not evidence of being them.

Opaque tokens; only the sha-256 hash is stored, matching Phase 11's sessions.token_hash column, because a stolen database should not be a stolen session. Access life 10 minutes, refresh 30 days, with a 90-day absolute ceiling on the whole chain -- without it a weekly-refreshed session never ends, which is a password that types itself.

Every refresh retires the old token. Presenting a retired one raises TokenTheftSuspected and revokes the ENTIRE family: either it was stolen or it was replayed, and both mean the chain is no longer trustworthy. Deliberately harsher than convenient.

revoke_session cascades to the family, revoke_user covers every family, and both take effect on the next verify with no cache to outlive them. inventory() lists live sessions per user and shows nothing of another user's.

Two mechanisms: a hard per-source limit (a source making hundreds of attempts is an attacker whatever account it names) and per-account exponential backoff capped at two minutes, never a lockout -- locking would hand an attacker a way to lock any account they can name. A success clears the account's backoff and not the source's limit.

CookiePolicy refuses to exist without HttpOnly and Secure, and refuses SameSite=None without Secure. CSRF is double-submit with constant-time comparison, required for cookie-bearing state changes and NOT for bearer tokens -- requiring it there would be a ritual without a defence.

Three signals, each a fact the system already has: a retired token presented again, a revoked session still being presented, and a session appearing from a new source while another is active. The third is surfaced, not acted on -- two computers is ordinary.

Registered with assurance levels and a production_requires line naming exactly what a real verifier needs. A mechanism is usable when a verifier is INSTALLED rather than when a flag says implemented -- a boolean claiming yes while no verifier exists is the kind of claim this program has already been bitten by.

Suspicious-session detection is three explicit signals, not intelligence. Nothing geolocates, fingerprints or models behaviour, and the source is an opaque hash supplied by the caller.

14.name: Device Identity

requirements.evidence: UserIdentity, DeviceIdentity and Attestation are distinct types that cannot be passed for one another. DeviceIdentity holds no user; Attestation holds neither a key nor a user. A jailbroken phone with a genuine key is a real device running an app nobody can vouch for, and the record says exactly that instead of collapsing it to trusted/untrusted.

There is no private-key field and no path that accepts one; a string that looks like a PEM private key is refused at construction, because somebody pasting one into the public field is not hypothetical. Hardware backing is recorded as a CLAIM the device makes, since the server cannot verify it by looking at a string.

A signed-in owner requests a challenge; the device signs owner|device_id|public_key|challenge. Signing the bare challenge would let a captured signature register a different device -- tested. Challenges are single-use, five-minute, and purpose-bound so a pairing challenge cannot be spent as a registration proof.

Ingest is idempotent by message id: the same message twice reports a duplicate, changes nothing, and leaves one row. The offline queue may deliver twice and the engine does not care -- a queue that guarantees exactly-once delivery does not exist.

recipients, subject, body, attachments -- held as REQUIRED_ON_SCREEN so that quietly dropping one is a test failure, and asserted to be exactly four. `on_screen()` is what the fingerprint hashes, so what is shown and what is signed cannot drift apart.

Tested for each of the four separately. The same shape as Phase 25 -- preview, fingerprint, approval carrying it, recompute at authorization -- reused deliberately rather than reinvented, because a second implementation of a rule that must hold in both places is a rule that will hold in one.

Hashed as a list, not a set. `to:` order is visible to every recipient, so a reordering that hashed the same would mean the approval covered a different-looking email. A mutation to `sorted()` is caught.

A policy ALLOW is not an approval and is refused; an approval cannot override a DENY. `delegated_policy` is refused naming Phase 50, and the refusal quotes the manifest's own example -- "send routine availability confirmations" -- so the shape Phase 50 will implement is written down rather than inferred.

A calendar write has an inverse; a sent email does not, for anybody, ever. `AuthorizedSend` carries `undo_available=False` and the reason as FIELDS rather than omitting them, because a caller that finds no undo field will assume one is coming.

Recipients and attachment count are recorded -- who an email went to is the whole question an audit trail of sending exists to answer. The body is not: a trail that keeps every sent message is a second mailbox, and Phase 6's redaction would have to strike it anyway. A refused send produces a record too, with actor `orion` rather than `user`.

Python 1322/1322 (was 1274). 48 tests across Phases 28-29. **The mutation harness had a defect found while closing these phases**: it restored a mutated file without disabling bytecode writing, and Python invalidates a `.pyc` on (mtime, size) at one-second resolution -- so a same-length swap (`RiskLevel.R3` to `R2`) restored within the same second left the cached MUTATED bytecode looking valid. That produced a phantom full-suite failure while the file on disk was correct. It can also produce a false CAUGHT, so no earlier verdict could be trusted. The harness now sets PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 and **all 104 guards from Phases 21-29 were re-run from scratch: 104 caught, 0 survived, 0 skipped.** Recorded in AGENTS.md's traps section. **Revised after the 2026-08-26 independent review:** Python 1375/1375. Four corrections, each mutation-tested.

limitations: **Nothing is sent.** `authorize_send` returns a PreparedRequest and an audit record. No MIME message is assembled, no transport exists, no email has left this machine.
The policy outcome is passed in, not computed -- same as Phase 25. Phase 5's engine is not reachable from the backend.
No approval expires, here or in Phase 25. The fingerprint binds WHAT was approved and nothing binds WHEN.
There is no rate limit and no send log. Nothing prevents the same approved preview being authorized repeatedly, which would send the same email many times -- an approval is not consumed by use.
Attachments are names. Nothing verifies that a named attachment exists or that its content is what the person saw.
`REQUIRED_ON_SCREEN` proves the preview CONTAINS the four. Nothing here can prove a UI displays them.

`require_person` compares the reviewer and approver against the `user_id` the caller passes in. It cannot verify that a human was actually present -- only that the names recorded are the account holder's and not a system actor. Real assurance needs the device-bound approval Phase 49 owns.

An approval is still not consumed by use: the same approved preview authorises the same send indefinitely. This was already a recorded follow-up and remains the highest-priority one before any transport exists.
followUps: **An approval must be single-use.** Right now the same approval authorises the same send indefinitely; a consumed-approval record is needed before any transport exists, or a retry loop becomes a mailing.
Approvals need a lifetime, across both Phase 25 and here.
Phase 50 inherits `delegated_policy` in two modules now. Whatever it allows must still produce the preview and the audit record: delegation removes the human step, not the trail.
A send log is needed for the audit trail to be complete -- currently a record is produced and nothing stores it.

postReviewCorrections.evidence: **The requirement's letter was satisfied and its purpose was not.** Nothing checked that the reviewer or approver was a person, that they differed, or that either matched the `user_id` `authorize_send` already receives. ORION reviewed its own draft, granted its own approval as `granted_by="orion"`, and the audit recorded `actor: "user"`. `require_person` now refuses system actor names and requires both to be the account holder; an approval predating the draft is refused too.

`Address.display_name` is attacker-chosen text any UI rendering `Name <addr>` will show, so an approval for `Google Security Team <bob@x.com>` validated for `Bob <bob@x.com>`. `draft_id` was unbound, so two drafts with identical content shared a fingerprint and an approval for one authorised the other. And `reply_to_differs` -- the redirect warning this phase built -- was neither shown on the approval screen nor hashed. All now in `on_screen()`, which is what the fingerprint hashes.

`risk: RiskLevel = SEND_RISK` was a field `authorize_send` never compared to the constant, so a preview could declare R1 and be audited as R1 -- an R3 action recorded as something else. The constant was pinned by a test and its USE was not. Phase 25 had the same shape and is fixed the same way.

The `ensure_ascii=True` surrogate-pair collision described under Phase 25 applied to the recipient address -- the one field where a mismatch is both unrecoverable and invisible. Closed at the `Address` boundary and in the encoding.

30.name: HealthKit Local Layer

requirements.evidence: sleep, resting heart rate, HRV, respiratory rate, steps, active energy, workouts, exercise minutes -- asserted as exactly those eight raw values, not as a count. `HealthType` being a closed enum IS the manifest's "do not request every HealthKit permission": there is no way to name a type outside it. A check asserts ORION asks for under a tenth of what HealthKit offers, and `HealthTypeCatalogue.neverRequested` names five categories with reasons -- clinical records, mental health, reproductive health, blood glucose, medications -- so the exclusions are a decision on the record rather than an omission.

`HealthDevice.mayReadHealth` is true for exactly one case, asserted by counting rather than by naming. The watch is excluded deliberately and the reason is in the source: Phase 77 is "Future Apple Watch Expansion", and a watch that started reading health data now would make that phase a migration rather than an addition. `request()` refuses on any other device.

`outstanding(from:)` returns only what has not been asked about; a second request for {sleep, steps, workouts} after a first for {sleep, steps} asks for workouts alone. Re-asking for something already answered is REFUSED, because a repeated permission sheet is a sheet people learn to dismiss.

**HealthKit will not tell an app whether READ access was granted.** Apple returns notDetermined or a write status; for reads, a denial and an empty data set are deliberately indistinguishable, so an app cannot detect that somebody declined. `HealthAuthorization.unknowable` is that state and it is the NORMAL outcome of a read request. Modelling it as `granted` would produce exactly the bug AGENTS.md already records -- *missing health data is not zero* -- at the authorization layer instead of the scoring layer.

`HealthReading` has three cases, not two. `HealthLocalLayer.interpret` is the ONE function that decides what an empty array means, so the decision is in one place rather than at every call site that receives one. `contributes()` returns false for `noData` and for `notAuthorized`: a person who did not wear their watch has no resting heart rate, and scoring that as zero tells them they had a bad day because a device did not sync.

Distinguished from `denied` because what happens next differs. Revocation says ORION may no longer read NEW data; it does not say the person wants their history erased, and a re-grant an hour later should find it where they left it -- the same position Phase 22 took on a revoked OAuth grant. A mutation that resets the ledger on revoke is caught.

`HealthSample` is not Codable, and neither is `HealthType`, so making the sample serialisable takes TWO deliberate edits rather than one -- the one-line version does not compile, and the two-line version is caught by a runtime assertion that the type is not Encodable or Decodable. Phase 17's cache rules already list `health_state` as never cached; this is the same rule at the other end of the wire.

Phase 16 built `Deferred.swift` and had MobileCoreCheck grep every source for HealthKit, HKHealthStore and HKQuery. That check was SUPPOSED to fail now. Releasing it by hand-editing two parallel lists is how the other two features get released by accident later, so `forbiddenTokens` is now DERIVED from `features`: a feature carries its own tokens, removing the feature removes them together. HealthKit moves to a `released` list rather than being deleted, so the record shows a decision. Four new invariants are asserted, including that a still-deferred feature cannot have lost its tokens and that a released one still records what it was identified by. Gmail and remote Mac control remain locked.

The iOS simulator build passes with no source change. This phase defines the PORT -- authorization ledger, requested type set, sample and reading shapes -- and `RefusingHealthStore` raises rather than returning plausible numbers, the same position Phase 12 took with the cipher and Phase 16 with the secure store.

The assertion that a released feature's tokens are no longer forbidden passed when the token list was emptied, because `allSatisfy` over an empty collection is true. A feature could have been released by deleting its tokens rather than by deciding to release it. Now paired with an assertion that a released feature still names them.

Swift **140 checks, 0 failed** (was 103); iOS simulator build clean. Python 1322/1322 unaffected. native/Orion 318 XCTest cases, 0 failures. Plugin 146/146. All eight check scripts clean; secret scan clean. Seventeen Swift guards mutation-tested: 16 caught by assertion, 1 by the compiler, and the one survivor was the vacuous check above, now closed and re-mutated. **Revised after the 2026-08-26 independent review:** Swift **152 checks, 0 failed** (was 140); iOS simulator build clean. Seven corrections; the not-Encodable claim restated rather than repaired, because Swift cannot prevent a retroactive conformance.

limitations: **No HealthKit adapter exists.** `RefusingHealthStore` is the only implementation. Nothing has read a single sample, on any device, ever -- this is the local layer's shape and rules, not a working integration.
There is no SwiftUI. Phase 16's deviation stands: the mobile phases produce a compiled domain layer and no app, and Phase 34 is 'ORION Health UI' with nothing to build on yet.

`HealthAuthorizationLedger` is in-memory. Nothing persists which types were requested, so a restart would re-ask -- which is the exact failure the incremental-request rule exists to avoid, and it is unfixable without the storage layer.

`HealthTypeCatalogue.approximateAvailableTypes` is 100, a deliberate lower bound rather than a real count of HealthKit's type catalogue. The comparison it supports is 'a small fraction', which is true at any plausible real number.
Nothing reads data yet, so 'keep raw historical data local' is currently true because there is no data. The property that will matter is the absence of an encoder, which is asserted now.
`HealthSample` carries a raw Double and a unit string. Unit correctness is not checked -- minutes and hours of sleep are the same type here.

Denied vs unknowable cannot be distinguished for reads by design, so `needsAttention` will only ever surface WRITE denials and explicit revocations. A person who silently declined a read type is indistinguishable from one with no data, and ORION cannot tell them why a number is missing.

**`HealthSample` not being Codable prevents the SYNTHESISED encoder and nothing more.** A review exfiltrated one four ways without touching MobileCore: `String(describing:)`, `Mirror`, reading the five public properties, and `extension HealthSample: @retroactive Encodable` in any other module -- which the in-process assertion cannot see, because it only observes conformances linked into the checking binary. Swift has no way to prevent a retroactive conformance. The guard is real and its reach is one module.
`HealthTypeCatalogue.approximateAvailableTypes` is 100, a deliberate lower bound and not a count of HealthKit's real type catalogue. The assertion it supports compares against a hand-picked constant.
followUps: Phase 31 (Health Baseline Engine) must exclude absent inputs rather than scoring them zero -- `HealthLocalLayer.contributes` exists for it to use, and `SessionDomain/DayScore.swift` already does this on the Mac side. Two implementations of that rule is how they come to disagree.

Phase 33 (Health Privacy Firewall) inherits the not-Codable property. If it needs any health value to reach the backend, the derived, non-raw form is what crosses -- and the encoder must live there, not on HealthSample.
The authorization ledger needs persistence before the incremental-request rule is real.
When an HKHealthStore adapter is written it belongs in a platform target that MobileCore does not import, or the iOS-build discipline that has held since Phase 16 is spent.

postReviewCorrections.evidence: **One of the two reasons the phase was judged not complete as claimed.** `HealthAuthorizationLedger.device` was written once and read by nothing: the guard consulted the `on:` PARAMETER, so a ledger constructed for `.mac` authorized happily when told `on: .iPhone`, and the two values disagreed with the stored one losing silently. Re-pointing the guard at `self.device` was a mutation that survived at 140/0. Worse, `settle` and `revoke` had NO device gate at all, so a watch ledger reached `readable` without ever calling `request()`.

`outstanding` filters on `.notRequested`, so a revoked type could not be asked for again -- and the only path back to readable was the ungated `settle`, with no request, no permission sheet and no device check. Re-granting is a decision, so it is now its own named call, `reopen()`.

`.requested` -- the sheet is up and nothing is known -- returned `.notAuthorized`, which says the person refused. And `.revoked` discarded samples already held, throwing away the local history this phase explicitly says revocation keeps, at the one place a caller would look for it. "Never zero" held throughout.

`(try? String(contentsOf:)) ?? ""` treated an unreadable file as empty. The review chmod-ed a source to 000 with a forbidden token in it and the check went green. A grep that cannot read its input has not checked it.

`features.allSatisfy { $0.tokens.allSatisfy(forbiddenTokens.contains) }` while `forbiddenTokens` IS `features.flatMap(\.tokens)` -- true by construction. Dropping "GmailAPI" from Gmail's three tokens survived at 140/0, so a still-deferred feature could lose its identifiers unnoticed. The expected contents are now pinned literally. This phase self-reported one vacuous assertion in this area and there were three.
`neverRequested` could name "steps" while `HealthType.steps` was still requested -- an exclusion list that flatly contradicts the code and therefore says nothing. Now asserted disjoint.

Not repaired, because Swift cannot prevent it -- corrected instead. The gate said raw data "cannot leave because it cannot be encoded" and described making the type Codable as "TWO deliberate edits". Both mutations ARE caught, as claimed. But the review exfiltrated a sample four ways without touching MobileCore -- `String(describing:)`, `Mirror`, reading the public properties, and `extension HealthSample: @retroactive Encodable` in any other module, which the in-process assertion cannot see. The property prevents the SYNTHESISED encoder and nothing more. Restated accurately in `limitations`.

31.name: Health Baseline Engine

requirements.evidence: sleep duration, sleep consistency, resting HR, HRV, activity and training load -- asserted as exactly those six raw values, not as a count. Adding a seventh fails to compile against the exhaustive `step(for:at:)` switch, which is the compiler doing the work a test would otherwise have to.
In MobileCore, next to Phase 30's local layer. The data is already local and deliberately not encodable; computing baselines on a server would mean first inventing a way for the samples to leave.

Seven observations, and below it there is NO baseline -- `nil`, asserted for every count from zero to six, for both `baseline()` and `sleepConsistency()`. The same shape as Phase 21's estimate learner: a confident wrong number is worse than an absent one because it looks earned.

A resting heart rate of 58.3719 from six readings claims a thousandth of a beat. Values and spreads are quantised to a step that WIDENS as confidence falls, so a provisional baseline reads as provisional without a caveat attached. The monotonicity is asserted for all six kinds rather than for one example, and a test proves the reported value sits on its own step.

One two-hour night after a flight is not a fact about how somebody sleeps. Tested: seven eight-hour nights plus one two-hour night leaves the baseline at 480 minutes, and replacing the median with a mean is caught.

The usual implementation of "do not compare users against generic population scores" is a fallback -- which then gets used every time the personal baseline is missing, exactly when the comparison is least useful and most likely to be believed. There is no constant to fall back to; a missing baseline is nil. Same rule as AGENTS.md's *missing health data is not zero*, one level up.

A fortnight-wide window containing eight nights yields sampleCount 8 and the median of those eight -- not a value dragged down by six zeros. This is the rule `SessionDomain/DayScore.swift` already implements on the Mac, and the one AGENTS.md records the consequence of getting wrong.

A baseline recomputed this morning from data that stopped arriving three weeks ago is three weeks old. Freshness is measured from the newest CONTRIBUTING sample, so a watch that stopped syncing cannot produce a baseline that looks current forever. Staleness CAPS confidence rather than averaging into it: a hundred readings that all stopped a month ago do not describe today, and averaging would let the sample size hide it.

Two questions that get collapsed constantly -- somebody sleeping a steady seven hours from 02:00 has excellent duration and poor consistency, and only one of those is actionable tonight. A steady 02:00 scores zero variation however late it is. **Midnight is not a discontinuity**: bedtimes alternating 23:50 and 00:10 are twenty minutes of variation, not twenty-three hours.

Acute (7d) against chronic (28d, normalised per week). When chronic load is zero the ratio is ABSENT -- not 1.0 and not infinity: "no ratio" and "a ratio of one" mean opposite things, and a division that can produce a special value is a division that will.

low / moderate / high, from sample count and freshness. `confidence: 0.8137` is precision about uncertainty, which is the same fabrication one level up -- and Phase 32 asks for categories over meaningless decimal scores for this reason.

Swift **293 checks, 0 failed** (was 204). **Revised after the 2026-08-26 review of Phases 31-32:** six corrections, each mutation-tested, including a NaN ratio that crashed its consumer and a quantised spread that fabricated certainty. Of the review's 14 Phase 31 survivors, all are now caught except the calendar guard, which is unreachable and recorded as such.

limitations: **Nothing supplies samples.** Phase 30's store still refuses, so every baseline here is computed from fixtures. No baseline has been derived from a real person's data.
Nothing persists a baseline, so every one is recomputed from whatever the caller holds.

The constants are eight judgements in eight numbers: sampleFloor (7), moderateSamples (10), highSamples (21), staleAfter (7d), veryStaleAfter (21d), the acute/chronic windows (7d/28d), and the quantisation table. Their ORDERING is asserted; their absolute values are not defensible beyond producing the behaviour the manifest describes.
Training load sums whatever `value` the workout samples carry, with no notion of intensity. A gentle two-hour walk and a two-hour interval session are the same load here.
Sleep consistency reads the START of a sleep sample. It says nothing about wake time, which is the half a person can usually control less.

`activity` has no dedicated builder -- it goes through the generic `baseline()` like resting HR and HRV. Steps and active energy are both `activity` to this module, which is coarser than the eight types Phase 30 requests.
A baseline is not Encodable, which carries the same caveat Phase 30 records: that prevents the synthesised encoder and not a retroactive conformance in another module.

**Sleep consistency is approximate for an antipodal distribution.** The circular median is computed by unwrapping around a LINEAR median anchor, which is right for a cluster or a drift and wrong for two clusters roughly twelve hours apart: the anchor lands between them and the reported spread is large where the true circular spread is small. The review's 20,000-case differential search found no case exceeding the circular maximum, so nothing is nonsensical -- but bimodal sleep is reported worse than it is.

**MAD collapses to zero for any minority pattern under half.** Six nights at 23:00 and four at 01:00 report zero variation. That is a property of the median absolute deviation, chosen deliberately for robustness, and its cost is that it cannot see a minority habit at all.
The `?? 0` calendar guard is now a `guard` returning nil and is not reachable through `Calendar`'s public behaviour, so it is unenforced by any test.
followUps: Phase 32 derives states from these baselines and must carry `reason`, `baseline`, `confidence` and `freshness` through -- all four are on `Baseline` already, so the state should reference the baseline rather than copying its numbers.
Phase 33's firewall must pass DERIVED states to the planner and never a `Baseline`, which still carries a raw value and unit.
The authorization ledger and the baselines both need persistence before either rule is real.
`activity` should split into steps and active energy when something actually consumes it; one baseline for two units is a unit bug waiting to happen.

postReviewCorrections.evidence: **The requirement `training_load_has_no_ratio_without_a_denominator` was false as written**, and its own sentence -- "a division that can produce a special value is a division that will" -- describes what happened. `trainingLoad` had no `isFinite` filter, unlike `baseline()` twenty lines above it, so an infinite sample made acute and chronic both infinite, `chronic > 0` passed, and the ratio was NaN. Phase 32's `Int((ratio * 100).rounded())` then trapped: **Fatal error: Double value cannot be converted to Int**. Now filtered for finite AND non-negative, and the ratio must itself be finite. A negative session separately produced a chronic of 0.025 and a ratio of 28,000.

The gate said "values AND spreads are quantised", which was true and was the defect. A person sleeping 466-494 minutes has a real spread of 14; quantised at low confidence it reported **0**, the consumer's `max(spread, 1)` floor made that one minute, and a fifteen-minute difference became `wellBelowBaseline`. That fabricates CERTAINTY -- the same sin as fabricating precision, pointed the other way, in the phase built to prevent it. `spread` is now unquantised and is what comparison uses; `reportedSpread` is the rounded one, for display only; and `comparisonSpread` floors on the kind's own finest step rather than a bare 1 -- one bpm and one step are not comparable quantities.

`baseline()` filtered non-finite values and not future ones, while `trainingLoad` filtered the future -- so a baseline built entirely from samples dated ahead of `now` returned freshness 0.0 and `isStale == false`. The review found it by noticing the check hedged `acuteSamples == 8 || acuteSamples == 7`: the fixture's most recent night ENDED seven hours after `now`, so "twenty sessions" contributed nineteen. Both the code and every fixture are fixed, and the OR hedge is now an equality.

The gate describes "chronic (28d, normalised per week)" and removing the division left the checks green -- the only assertion was that the ratio was non-nil. Dropping it turns the check's own fixture from `heavy` to `light`. The acute total, the chronic total and the ratio are now all asserted by value.

The tight 23:50/00:10 fixture only reaches the `> 720` branch, because the median absolute deviation of a 50/50 split is insensitive to the other one. A bedtime DRIFTING from 22:20 to 01:20 reaches both, and both mutations are now caught.

`(components.hour ?? 0)` turned an unanswerable date into 00:00, so garbage dates would report perfect consistency. Now a `guard` returning nil. **Not covered by a test**: `Calendar.dateComponents([.hour, .minute])` returns values for every Date reachable through the public API, including `distantPast`, so the branch cannot be exercised. Recorded rather than claimed.

31.note: Planned 2026-08-26, implemented and closed 2026-08-27. The gate originally recorded 2026-08-26 for both because the session began on the 25th and the date was inferred rather than checked -- the trap AGENTS.md records.

32.name: ORION Health State

requirements.evidence: sleep_state, physical_recovery, physical_load, energy_state, stress_trend and data_confidence. The first five are closed enums, each with an `unknown` member; the sixth is Phase 31's `BaselineConfidence`.

There is no number on a state at all. A "recovery score of 73" implies a precision four nights of sleep cannot support, and people act on it. Even the confidence is a category -- `confidence: 0.8137` is precision about uncertainty, which is the same fabrication one level up.

`reason`, `baseline`, `confidence` and `freshness` are constructor parameters and the initialiser is failable: an empty reason returns nil. Four optional fields are four fields that are nil the first time somebody is in a hurry, and a state that cannot answer "why do you say that?" is one a person cannot argue with. `baseline` is the Phase 31 `Baseline` itself, not a copy of its numbers -- copying two of five is how they come to disagree.

"Do not represent these states as diagnoses" is a rule about words, and words are the one thing a type can hold exactly. `ClinicalVocabulary.forbidden` holds 22 stems and is checked, case-insensitively, against every reason AND every state value. The check runs over ORION's OWN vocabulary rather than filtering user input: the failure it prevents is not somebody typing "insomnia", it is ORION deciding to. A state that cannot spell a diagnosis cannot deliver one.

Asserted for all four derived states separately, and asserted specifically NOT to be the middle member. A `moderate` produced by having no data is indistinguishable from a `moderate` produced by measurement, and only one of them should change a plan. An unknown also carries `confidence: .low` and a reason naming which input was missing.

How far from baseline counts as unusual is measured in multiples of that person's own spread. Tested with two sleepers and the same night: an hour off is `wellBelowBaseline` for somebody who never varies and `atBaseline` for somebody who varies by two hours. This is the same instinct as Phase 31's refusal to keep a population table.

A picture built from one solid baseline and one provisional one is provisional. Averaging lets the good input hide the bad one and the person acts on the average. Freshness composes the same way -- the picture is as old as its oldest part, tested with a twenty-day-stale HRV baseline against a fresh resting heart rate.
`stressTrend` takes a recent and an earlier baseline and returns `unknown` without both. One window is a reading, not a direction.

Swift **293 checks, 0 failed** (was 243). **Revised after the 2026-08-26 review:** the original claim -- "fourteen guards mutation-tested; one survived" -- was true of the fourteen chosen and not of the file, where 23 of 42 survived. 41 assertions added, consuming real Phase 31 baselines; all 24 re-run mutations caught.

limitations: **Nothing supplies real data.** Phase 30's store refuses, Phase 31's baselines come from fixtures, and these states are derived from those. No state has been computed about a real person.

`stress_trend` is derived from comparing two baselines of the same kind over different periods, and nothing here constructs those two windows -- the caller must. There is no stress metric as such; HRV over time is the proxy, and that is a modelling choice this phase does not defend.

`physical_load` carries `baseline: nil` because `TrainingLoad` is not a `Baseline`. The manifest says preserve the baseline; for load the honest answer is that there is no single one, and the reason string carries the comparison instead.

The thresholds -- 1.0 and 2.0 spreads for departure, 1.3 and 0.8 for the load ratio -- are four judgements in four numbers, and the load ratios are borrowed from sports-science convention rather than derived from anything here.

`energyState` combines sleep and recovery with hand-written rules, not a model. It is deliberately conservative (it never returns `high` when either input is unknown) and it is a guess dressed as a category.
The clinical word list is 22 stems and is certainly incomplete. It catches ORION's own vocabulary drifting; it is not a guarantee that no phrasing anywhere reads as medical.
Nothing consumes a HealthState. Phase 33's firewall and Phase 34's UI are both empty, so these states are produced and read by nobody.

`HealthStateReading.baseline` is `Baseline?` and is nil for EVERY unknown state, not only for `physical_load` as the limitations previously implied. The manifest's "always preserve baseline" is satisfied in the sense that the field is always present and always accurate; it is not satisfied in the sense that a baseline always exists.
`energyState` combines sleep and recovery with five hand-written rules. Every branch is now tested, which makes it verified, not correct: it remains a guess dressed as a category.
followUps: Phase 33 must pass these DERIVED states to the planner and never a `Baseline` -- a Baseline still carries a raw value and a unit, which is exactly what the firewall exists to stop reaching the planner.
Phase 34 shows `reason` to a person. That string is the entire defence against this reading as a diagnosis, so the UI must not add wording of its own on top of it.
`physical_load` wanting a baseline it cannot have suggests `TrainingLoad` should expose its chronic figure as one.
The clinical word list should be re-read whenever a state gains a member, and the value check is what will catch the case where nobody does.

postReviewCorrections.evidence: **This is why the phase was judged not complete as claimed.** The gate's `verification` said "fourteen guards mutation-tested; one survived". That was true of the fourteen chosen and the file had 42, of which **23 survived** -- including the whole of `energyState` (hardwiring `.high` went unnoticed), `stressTrend`'s direction (reversing `building`/`easing` went unnoticed), the load thresholds, and all four divide-by-zero floors. The review named the structural cause exactly: **no Phase 32 assertion consumed a Phase 31-produced `Baseline`.** Every fixture was hand-built with a hand-chosen spread, so nothing exercised what the engine actually emits. Forty-one assertions were added over real baselines and every branch of every state function; all 24 re-run mutations are now caught.

Only `BaselineEngine.baseline` filtered non-finite values. The last sleep sample and both `latest*` readings arrived unvalidated, and three separate `Int(Double)` conversions trap on NaN or infinity -- one of them computed unconditionally, before the branch that would have made it benign. All three now go through a `usable()` check and return `unknown` instead of trapping.

`?? unknown(..., "the reason did not pass its own vocabulary check")` was true for one of the four things that can fail and a lie about the other three. A negative freshness silently turned a real `wellBelowBaseline` into `unknown` and blamed the word list. A wrong explanation is worse than a vague one, because somebody acts on it. Now "the inputs could not be read", with a test that it does not say "vocabulary".
The gate said 22 stems twice; there are 23. The only assertion was `count >= 20`, which pinned nothing. Now `== 23`, plus a duplicate check.

`a_trend_needs_two_windows` claimed `stressTrend` returns unknown "without both" and only tested without EITHER, so accepting a single window went unnoticed. And `a_state_with_no_evidence_is_unknown_not_a_middle_value` cited "load without a ratio is unknown, not steady" while the assertion passed no load object at all -- the `let ratio = load.ratio` half was unenforced, and a real ratio-less `TrainingLoad` is exactly the object Phase 31 is built to produce. Both halves are now tested, using a load the engine actually emits.

pendingGateAmendments.protocol: Do not silently reinterpret a manifest gate. Record it here when its text rests on an assumption the built system contradicts, keep working under a recorded deviation, and amend the manifest for all of them at once in a pass Nick reads end to end.

entries.gateText: Existing desktop ORION must run through ORION Core without meaningful behavioral regression.
entries.deadAssumption: That ORION Core is a running program the live route executes. It is a contract definition and reference validator; the live route is Swift -> OpenClaw -> TypeScript.
entries.proposedText: Existing desktop ORION must conform to ORION Core's contracts without meaningful behavioral regression: Core's schema-versioned envelopes must be proven to express a live capability end-to-end on the real route, and enabling that conformance check must leave user-visible output and durable audit evidence unchanged. Core defines and validates the contracts; platform adapters execute them.

entries.gateText: Support abstract model roles rather than hardcoded providers: reasoning, fast, vision, local, fallback, embedding
entries.deadAssumption: That `fallback` is a role. It is a property of a role -- a model is not the fallback model in the abstract, it is what a particular role falls back to. The list also omits speech-to-text and text-to-speech, which are model calls with credentials, latency and cost.
entries.proposedText: Support abstract model roles rather than hardcoded providers: reasoning, fast, vision, local, embedding, stt, tts. Each role declares its own ordered fallback chain.

scopeNotInManifest.protocol: The manifest is the requirements source. When Nick wants something it does not cover, record it here with what already exists and where it would belong, rather than either refusing it or silently building outside the document. Resolved in the same reviewed pass as pendingGateAmendments.

reviews.reviewer: an independent agent with no context of how the work was done, instructed to verify every claim rather than trust it
reviews.method: Mutation-tested 40 code sites, brute-forced the policy engine over 14,040 request shapes, ran bypass batteries against the redactor and the egress guard, and re-derived every number in this file from command output.
confirmed: All 12 (now 13) policy rules are load-bearing: removing any one fails a test.
No ALLOW above R2 in 14,040 request shapes.
The parity check reproduces exactly: 390/390, zero more permissive.
No job could be made to run twice or take an illegal transition.
Nothing was committed, pushed, or changed live; the plugin was untouched.
reviews.found: 2 HIGH, 1 HIGH-adjacent, 11 MEDIUM, 7 LOW and 5 NIT findings. Every one is recorded under the phase it belongs to, in postReviewCorrections, with the fix.
reviews.outcome: All findings addressed. Each fix was mutation-tested: the new test fails when the fix is removed. One newly written test was itself found vacuous (a Unicode fixture that replaced the wrong character) and rewritten until it bit.
reviews.note: The review's verdict was that Phases 5, 6, 8 were NOT complete as claimed and 9, 10 were weakened. That verdict was accepted rather than argued with; these entries are the repair.

reviews.method: Three independent agents with no context on how the work was done, given the manifest, the repo and the commands, and told to verify claims rather than trust them. Between them they ran roughly 190 mutations, fuzzed the planner over 400 random populations, and attacked the two approval fingerprints and the reply addressing path directly.

verdict.29: complete at the letter, with a serious inherited hole

reviews.outcome: Review ran 2026-08-26; the 36 corrections were applied 2026-08-27. Each was and each mutation-tested: remove the fix and a test fails. Eight repairs initially had no test that bit and were reworked until they did; two of those needed the scenario rebuilt because a cost check or a redundant guard was masking the branch under test. Python 1375/1375 (was 1322), Swift 152 checks (was 140). Corrections recorded per phase under postReviewCorrections rather than edited into the original evidence -- the fact that a claim was wrong is itself evidence about the evidence.
reviews.note: The single most serious finding was not a code defect: Phase 26's gate cited a 3,000-random-string differential test that did not exist in the repository. The run had happened in a shell and the conclusion was correct. Evidence nobody can re-run is not evidence, and this program's gate prose is written by whoever did the work with nothing checking it.

reviews.method: One oblivious agent, given the manifest, the repo and the commands. Built a throwaway Swift package with a path dependency on MobileCore to exercise it directly, then mutation-tested 82 guards across the two files.

verdict.31: complete, with one requirement untrue as written

reviews.outcome: 11 corrections applied and each mutation-tested. The most serious was a crash: trainingLoad had no isFinite filter, so an infinite sample produced a NaN ratio and Phase 32's Int() conversion trapped. The most instructive was structural -- no Phase 32 assertion consumed a Phase 31-produced Baseline, which is why 23 of 42 guards were unenforced and why a quantised spread that made a fifteen-minute difference read as a crisis was invisible. Swift 293 checks (was 243).
reviews.note: Third review in a row to find a gate claim that was false when written -- here a count ("22 stems", actually 23), a guard tested for 'without either' while claiming 'without both', and a requirement whose headline example was not the case the assertion exercised.

reviews.method: Six oblivious reviewers, one to three phases each; no implementer narrative supplied.
registeredNotRepaired: MobileCore Message has no revision field, so the phone resolves conflicts by arrival order while the server resolves by revision. Needs a Swift-side revision field and a conflict vector file; larger than a repair.
Throttle source_hash is caller-declared. Deriving it server-side requires the request pipeline, which does not exist.

No repository validates that a referenced row (for example messages.conversation_id) belongs to the same owner. The in-memory store has no foreign keys and there is no repository registry to resolve them through.
